column3: Establishes Talut's God-given authority before he leads the troops into the river test.
No clear contribution beyond a remote command to listen and speak carefully.
Frames victory as belonging to God's forces, supporting the later small group's confidence.
Directly pairs patient small numbers with victory over larger numbers by God's permission.
Opens the surrounding account with a fearful multitude, anticipating its concern with flight and numbers.
Shows how perceiving an enemy as many can produce failure and dispute before conflict.
Food selection and concealment offer only a distant comparison to the river's eating restriction.
God's choosing whom He wills lightly echoes the divine determination in the Talut account.
Denies that a faction can save apart from God, reinforcing reliance beyond troop strength.
Uses the same description of those certain of meeting their Lord who answer the fearful group in 2:249.
Sets the nearby narrative's command to fight in God's path before Talut's mobilization.
Its warning of a fitnah and harm only loosely illuminates the river as a trial.
Shows deliverance of a prophet and the believers with him, paralleling the faithful who pass on with Talut.
Provides no substantive link to the river test or its conflict.
The reward named al-ghurfah is unrelated to the permitted handful of water.
The immediate prelude anticipates that only a few will remain committed when fighting is required.
God's withholding and expanding only faintly resonates with the imposed restraint at the river.
Its bare mention of armies supplies little for reading the test or response.
Explicitly joins divine companionship to patience, the closing assurance of 2:249.
The next ayah shows the surviving group seeking patience, steadfastness, and help against Jalut.
Drinking imagery is detached from the river test's moral distinction.
Contrasts boastful assurance of victory with the God-centered confidence voiced in 2:249.
Completes the confirmation of Talut's leadership immediately before he tests the troops.
The image of two factions does not clarify the groups formed at the river.
Depicts companions in struggle who neither weaken nor submit, sharpening the patience in 2:249.
Supplies the immediate outcome: victory over Jalut comes by God's permission after the river crossing.
Drinking from boiling water does not illuminate the river test.
The phrase "from me" is too general to explain Talut's membership formula.
Extends the nearby account's account of conflict under God's will, but does not explain the test itself.
Names trial through fear and hunger and commands glad tidings for the patient, closely framing the ordeal.
Its food and drink as a sign offer only a distant material parallel.
Recalls a people once few becoming many, relevant to 2:249's contrast of small and large forces.
An arrogant leader and his troops deny return; the connection to Talut's trial is limited.
Rivers here are created provisions, not a test of obedience.
A commanded ordeal answered with obedience and patience closely parallels the river's separating test.
The shared verb for departure does not add to the military scene.
Meeting the Lord marks believers whom the prophet will not dismiss, supporting the identity of the faithful remnant.
Regulated eating in fasting offers a limited analogy for obedience through restraint.
Its attribution of misfortune to God only broadly relates to interpreting a trial.
Crossing the sea precedes idolatry, not a test like Talut's river command.
The sea crossing with Pharaoh's troops provides only a remote crossing-and-armies parallel.
Paradise rivers do not clarify the river test.
A battle scene where God tests inward states helps frame the river as a disclosure of the troops.
Its plea not to bear what exceeds capacity directly echoes the defeated group's claim of no capacity.
Commands believers facing a faction to stand firm and remember God, matching the later confrontation.
States that testing distinguishes strivers and the patient, clarifying the function of Talut's test.
A divinely set water-share rule supplies a close formal parallel to the river's regulated drinking.
Acceptance and pardon do not clarify the river test or battle.
Believers being with the prophet offers a distant parallel to those who believe with Talut.
The repeated call of Nuh has no material bearing on 2:249.
A bare statement of defeat offers little beyond the idea of reversal in conflict.
God grants tranquility to believers and owns all forces, supporting confidence beyond visible numbers.
Its dietary prohibitions do not explain the specific river limit.
Patience is named among the defining qualities of the faithful remnant.
Its concern with loyalties does not clarify the river test or the small force.
The general command for beautiful patience only lightly supports the closing praise of patience.
Its preference for patience is unrelated to Talut's military trial.
The adjective for dense gardens is unrelated to overcoming a force.
Divine signs come only by God's permission, a broad resonance with victory by His permission.
Patience and righteous works are rewarded, but the setting is not the contest in 2:249.
Its detailed debt procedure does not contribute to the river scene.
Calling from behind rooms does not illuminate 2:249.
Its command to verify on campaign is not tied to the river test or numerical fear.
Frequent remembrance broadly supports the God-conscious response, without a specific link.
Meeting God is connected to death here, not the faithful group's conviction in 2:249.
Competition in accumulation has no clear bearing on the passage.
Revelation by God's permission gives only a broad divine-agency parallel.
The contrast with few who give thanks weakly echoes the few who obey at the river.
Water is apportioned and each drinking turn assigned, closely paralleling a divinely regulated water access.
God decrees victory for Himself and His messengers, reinforcing the premise behind victory despite numbers.
The paradise rooms and rivers do not explain the river ordeal.
Names Israel's rescue from Pharaoh as a great trial, furnishing an Israelite pattern of ordeal and deliverance.
Subjection by God's permission is too remote from Talut's troop test.
The mention of Iblis's troops does not add to the passage.
Food-law exceptions do not clarify the river's selective command.
Eating and temporary enjoyment do not illuminate the trial.
The absence of a close companion is unrelated to the groups in 2:249.
Makes divine help, not opponents, decisive and commands believers to rely on God.
Shows an apparently secure force overcome unexpectedly by God, qualifying judgments based on visible strength.
Its praise of the patient and grateful is only a general moral resonance.
Being overcome by misery does not clarify the contest or test.
A future defeat warning gives only a generic conflict connection.
Its declaration about decisive speech does not contribute to 2:249.
Expansion and restriction of provision do not explain the controlled drinking.
God's protection and sovereignty broadly support the passage's reliance on Him.
God's possession of the forces of heaven and earth supports the claim that victory is not numerical.
Its discussion of divine giving and warfire does not clarify Talut's trial.
The wish to follow victors only faintly contrasts with 2:249's faithful confidence.
A battle outcome occurs by God's permission and exposes believers, paralleling trial within conflict.
Patience in waiting is a general but distant echo of the passage's patience.
Pilgrimage regulations do not add to the river test.
Daylight's disclosure has no substantive link to 2:249.
Its bounded permission to eat and drink offers a formal analogy to obedience within a defined limit.
Links permission to fight with God's power to give aid, grounding the conflict's reliance on divine help.
The general measure of recompense does not clarify the river or battle.
Calling to God by His permission does not add to the scene.
Its call to glorify God is not connected to Talut's test.
Patience is necessary for receiving divine reward, a general support for the closing quality.
The food image does not explain the river command.
Locates patience in God, supporting the passage's assurance that God is with the patient.
Names patience in hardship and at the time of battle, directly framing the quality praised in 2:249.
Depicts believers tested by hardship until they ask when God's help will come, matching the passage's ordeal and confidence in aid.
Places fighting under divine prescription despite human reluctance, supplying the larger obligation behind Talut's mobilization.
Links faith and striving in God's path with hope in His mercy, supporting the faithful group's response within the campaign.
Presents two confronting factions and warns that visible numbers can mislead, closely supporting 2:249's small-versus-large contrast.
Recalls divine aid at Badr when the believers were weak, directly reinforcing confidence beyond material strength.
Makes patient steadfastness a condition of divine aid against an attacking force, closely paralleling the closing assurance of 2:249.
Defines divine aid as reassurance for hearts and makes victory belong to God alone.
Forbids weakening and grief to believers, directly countering the despair voiced before Jalut.
Shows believers answering a threat of assembled forces with trust that God is sufficient.
Commands perseverance, mutual steadfastness, and readiness, furnishing a direct ethical frame for the remnant.
Joins seeking help from God with patience and places the outcome under His control.
Calls a persecuted people to patience while their Lord may destroy their enemy and make them successors.
Shows believers seeking aid and receiving divine reinforcement before battle.
Makes God's aid reassurance and tranquility, while declaring that victory comes only from Him.
Commands steadfastness when believers meet an advancing force.
Defines turning away on the day of encounter as a grave failure, sharpening the contrast with those who cross on.
Commands obedience, rejects dispute that causes failure, and ends with God being with the patient.
Directly states that a patient smaller force can overcome a much larger force by God's permission.
Warns that numerical abundance can fail to benefit a force, directly qualifying the fear of Jalut's troops.
Pairs divine tranquility and unseen forces with victory after numerical confidence fails.
God's presence with the threatened companion and His unseen forces reinforce confidence under danger.
States that God does not waste the reward of those who are mindful and patient.
Associates God's signs with every enduring, grateful person, supporting the passage's patient few.
Promises that God will surely help those who help His cause, grounding hope for aid in conflict.
Recalls believers facing forces and receiving divine intervention, a close battle-and-aid parallel.
Shows believers meeting the confederate forces with increased faith and submission rather than despair.
Promises help to messengers and believers in worldly life, supporting the confidence of the faithful group.
Makes God's support responsive to believers' support of His cause and promises to make their feet firm.
Forbids weakness and calling for compromise while God is with believers, answering the posture of defeatism.
Foretells that the gathered force will be defeated and turn away, reinforcing the reversibility of visible military advantage.
Links revealed guidance with the balance and iron, situating force within divine justice rather than numbers alone.
Praises those who fight in God's path in a solid rank, sharpening the disciplined unity lacking in a failing force.
Ends with a believing group overcoming its enemy through divine support.
Promises sufficiency to whoever relies on God, reinforcing the remnant's God-centered assurance.
